title: Trump's Blue Reflecting Pool Turns Green—Scientists Say It Was Inevitable
summary: The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was supposed to showcase a pristine "American flag blue" bottom after a multi-million-dollar renovation ordered by President Trump. Instead, it's become a vivid green—the result of a massive algae bloom that scientists say was practically guaranteed. "It's called 'New Pond Syndrome,'" explained Steve Goodale, a Canadian swimming pool specialist known online as "Swimming Pool Steve." "It's a known thing that happens when you take a natural, clear body of water like this that sits in an open air environment and you try to start it up, very often you end up with green water almost immediately." The pool, which stretches 2,030 feet and covers about 338,000 square feet, took days to turn green likely due to its sheer size. Rosalina Stancheva Christova, a professor of aquatic ecology at George Mason University, took water samples and confirmed the algae is Desmodesmus, a common, non-toxic genus. She said the pool provides "excellent conditions" for algae: shallow, stagnant water, strong sunlight, and no shade. "It could happen every single summer," she added. "But it seems that the disturbance of the pond during the renovations [is] accelerating this process." The new dark blue interior is also a factor. "The new, darker interior surface is going to absorb more sunlight," Goodale said. "It is going to result in water that's warmer, and that ultimately is going to lead to more prolific algae growth." The Trump administration attributed the bloom to residual material in dormant supply lines, exacerbated by extreme heat that pushed heat index values above 95 degrees. An Interior Department spokesperson noted that algae has "long plagued the Reflecting Pool since 1922" and pointed to a similar outbreak after a 2012 renovation under President Obama. "Unlike under Obama and Biden, the National Park Service is actually maintaining the beautifully completed Reflecting Pool," they added. To combat the bloom, workers are pouring hydrogen peroxide—a milder alternative to chlorine—into the water and deploying "high-tech nanobubble ozone technology" to neutralize algae and pathogens. The department says this approach is validated by several universities and NOAA. This isn't the first green-out: in 2019, crews drained four million gallons to fix an algae-filled broken water line. For now, the iconic pool remains a very un-presidential shade of green, a reminder that even the most carefully planned renovations can't outsmart nature.
why_it_matters: It shows that even the most famous human-made landmarks are subject to basic ecological rules—prestige and political branding don't stop algae from growing when conditions are right.

background_read: The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is a iconic long pool on the National Mall in Washington D.C., built in the 1920s; Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech overlooking it in 1963.
Large, shallow pools of still water naturally warm up quickly in sunlight, creating ideal conditions for algae—an ecological rule that has challenged park services for decades.
The idea of 'New Pond Syndrome' is well known to pond and aquarium owners worldwide: new water bodies often go through a murky green phase before bacteria and plants establish a natural balance.
Rosalina Stancheva Christova is an aquatic ecology professor at George Mason University who studies how microorganisms like algae react to environmental changes in public waters.

NOAA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, is the U.S. agency mentioned as helping validate the nanobubble treatment—though algae problems in a reflecting pool are not their usual focus, it shows the extent of the effort.

perspectives.description: The Trump administration quickly implemented advanced treatment methods and publicly argued that they were improving on past neglect. Supporters might see this as proof they take maintenance seriously.

Critics point out that choosing a dark bottom for an open-air shallow pool made a green bloom almost certain—a basic science mistake. The statement dismissing previous administrations feels more about politics than park care.
Algae are a natural part of still water ecosystems. This bloom is not a political scandal but a recurring maintenance issue faced by every reflecting pool on Earth, regardless of who is president.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: Designing with nature in mind
perspectives.description: If the pool needs constant chemical dosing every summer, future renovations might reconsider the color and depth to work with, not against, natural sunlight and biology. This case could educate the public on sustainable landscaping.
